learn: The elements of art are the building blocks artists use: line, shape, form, value, colour, space and texture.
Lines can be straight, curved, thick, thin, implied or expressive. Shapes are flat (2D); forms are 3D.
Geometric shapes have exact edges; organic shapes are free and natural.
lessons.try: Fill a page with ten different kinds of line.

learn: Value is how light or dark a tone is.
Colour has hue (its name), value and intensity (brightness or dullness).
Texture is how something feels or looks like it feels: rough, smooth, soft.
check: Feels or looks like it feels
lessons.try: Make rubbings of five textures around your home.

learn: Positive space is the subject; negative space is the area around it.
Artists show depth by overlapping, changing size and placing objects higher on the page.
Negative space can make a picture balanced and clear.
check: The area around a subject is...
lessons.try: Draw a chair by drawing only the negative spaces around it.

learn: Principles of design describe how elements are arranged: balance, emphasis, contrast, rhythm, movement, unity and proportion.
Symmetrical balance is the same on both sides; asymmetrical balance uses different items of equal visual weight.
Emphasis is the focal point that draws the eye first.
check: Different items of equal visual weight
lessons.try: Make an asymmetrically balanced collage.

learn: Contrast places opposites together: light and dark, big and small.
Rhythm repeats elements to create a visual beat.
Movement guides the viewer's eye through the artwork.
lessons.try: Design a pattern with a strong rhythm.

learn: Unity makes an artwork feel complete, with parts that belong together.
Proportion is the size relationship between parts, like head size compared to the body.
An adult figure is about seven to eight heads tall.
check: An adult is about ___ heads tall.
lessons.try: Draw a figure using head-length measurements.

learn: Observational drawing means drawing what you actually see, not what you think something looks like.
Slow down, look more than you draw, and measure with your pencil held at arm's length.
Contour drawing traces the edges of an object.
lessons.try: Do a five-minute contour drawing of your hand.

learn: In blind contour drawing, you look only at the object, not the paper.
Gesture drawing captures movement and pose quickly, in 30 seconds to two minutes.
These exercises train the connection between eye and hand.
check: In blind contour drawing, you look at the...
lessons.try: Do five 30-second gesture drawings of a friend posing.

learn: A still life is an arrangement of objects like fruit, bottles or flowers.
Artists like Paul Cézanne (1839-1906) painted many still lifes of apples.
Start with light outlines, then add value and detail.
lessons.try: Set up and draw a still life of three objects.

learn: A value scale goes from white through greys to black.
Highlights are the lightest areas; core shadows are the darkest parts of an object.
Cast shadows fall on surfaces away from the light.
check: The lightest area on an object is the...
On a surface away from the light
lessons.try: Make a nine-step value scale with pencil.

learn: Hatching uses parallel lines; cross-hatching layers lines in different directions.
Stippling uses dots; blending smooths tones.
More lines or dots make darker values.
lessons.try: Shade four circles using four techniques.

learn: Shading turns shapes into forms: a circle becomes a sphere.
Decide where the light comes from and keep it consistent.
Reflected light is a faint lighter area inside the shadow.
check: Shading turns a circle into a...
lessons.try: Draw and shade a sphere, cube and cylinder.

learn: Primary colours (red, yellow, blue) mix to make secondary colours (orange, green, violet).
Tertiary colours mix a primary and a neighbouring secondary, like red-orange.
The colour wheel shows these relationships in a circle.
lessons.try: Paint a 12-part colour wheel.

learn: Complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel: red and green, blue and orange.
Analogous colours sit side by side: blue, blue-green, green.
Monochromatic uses one hue with tints (adding white) and shades (adding black).
lessons.try: Paint the same small scene in two different colour schemes.

learn: Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel energetic and seem to come forward.
Cool colours (blue, green, violet) feel calm and seem to recede.
Artists use colour to create mood, as in Vincent van Gogh's "The Starry Night" (1889).
lessons.try: Make two small paintings: one warm, one cool.

learn: Atmospheric perspective makes far objects lighter, bluer and less detailed.
Near objects are darker, brighter and sharper.
This mimics how air affects what we see over long distances.
lessons.try: Paint three layers of mountains, fading as they go back.

learn: Linear perspective uses a horizon line and vanishing points.
In one-point perspective, parallel lines meet at a single vanishing point.
Renaissance artists like Filippo Brunelleschi developed this method in the 1400s.
check: In one-point perspective, lines meet at...
Linear perspective was developed in the...
lessons.try: Draw a road or hallway in one-point perspective.

learn: Two-point perspective uses two vanishing points on the horizon line.
It is used to draw objects seen from a corner, like a building.
Vertical lines stay vertical.
check: Two-point perspective is used for objects seen...
In two-point perspective, vertical lines stay...
lessons.try: Draw a box in two-point perspective, then turn it into a building.

learn: Printmaking transfers an image from a prepared surface to paper, often many times.
Each print is called an impression; a set is an edition.
Prints let artists share work widely.
check: A set of prints is an...
lessons.try: Make a simple print by pressing a painted leaf onto paper.

learn: In relief printing, you carve away areas; the raised parts take the ink.
Japanese woodblock printers like Katsushika Hokusai made "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" (about 1831).
Foam sheets can be pressed with a pencil for safe relief prints.
check: In relief printing, the ___ parts take ink.
A safe material for school relief prints is...
lessons.try: Make a foam-sheet relief print.

learn: Stencils block ink from some areas to make sharp shapes.
A monoprint is a one-of-a-kind print made from a painted smooth surface.
Reversal matters: letters must be carved or drawn backwards.
lessons.try: Make a stencil print with cut paper.

learn: Sculpture in the round can be seen from all sides; relief sculpture projects from a flat surface.
Additive sculpture builds up material; subtractive sculpture carves away.
Michelangelo's "David" (1504) was carved from a single block of marble.
check: Sculpture seen from all sides is...
lessons.try: Make a small additive sculpture with clay.

learn: Pinch pots are formed by pinching a ball of clay.
Coil building uses rolled ropes of clay; slab building uses flat sheets.
Score and slip (scratch and wet) to join clay pieces.
lessons.try: Make a pinch pot or coil pot.

learn: Assemblage combines found objects into art.
Paper can be folded, curled and cut into 3D forms.
Artists consider balance and how the work looks from all sides.
check: Paper sculpture can be made by...
Sculptors consider how work looks from...
lessons.try: Build a sculpture from recycled cardboard.

learn: Ancient Egyptian art showed figures in profile with eyes from the front.
Ancient Greek sculptors aimed for idealised human forms.
Chinese ink painting values brushwork and landscapes.
lessons.try: Draw yourself in the Egyptian style.

learn: West African masks are carved for ceremonies and dances.
Aboriginal Australian art uses dot patterns and symbols for stories.
Native American art includes pottery, beadwork and weaving.
check: Many West African masks are used in...
lessons.try: Design a pattern inspired by dot painting with your own symbols.

learn: The Renaissance (1400s-1500s) brought realism and perspective: Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael.
Impressionism (1870s) captured light and moments: Claude Monet.
Cubism (1900s) showed many views at once: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque.
lessons.try: Paint a scene in the Impressionist style with quick brushstrokes.

learn: Art critique has four steps: describe, analyse, interpret, judge.
Describe what you see; analyse how elements and principles are used.
Interpret the meaning; judge the success with reasons.
check: The first step of critique is...
lessons.try: Critique a famous painting using all four steps.

learn: Helpful feedback is specific, kind and useful.
Use "I notice...", "I wonder..." and "What if...?"
Focus on the work, not the person.
lessons.try: Give a classmate two specific compliments and one suggestion.

learn: An artist statement explains what you made, how and why.
A portfolio collects your best work to show growth.
Reflecting helps you set goals as an artist.
lessons.try: Write a short artist statement for one of your works.
